claim: Anthropic's repo states that a deterministic algorithm solves 3-SAT in 2^{o(n)} time, which refutes ETH.
quote: A deterministic algorithm solves 3-SAT on n variables in time 2^{o(n)}, which refutes the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH).

claim: Anthropic says the result is purely asymptotic and has no practical use.
quote: The result is purely asymptotic and says nothing about solving formulas in practice.

claim: An internal research Claude model discovered the result, and AI models wrote the Lean 4 formalization.
quote: This folder holds the paper and its Lean 4 formalization, which was written by AI models.

claim: The core algorithm was found on October 16 by an internal Claude model, using 14M output tokens and no human input. Humans then helped with the presentation.
quote: The core algorithm was found on October 16 by an internal Claude research model with 14M output tokens and no human input. Anthropic researchers worked with Claude to improve the presentation, resulting in this paper.

claim: Anthropic's paper acknowledges OpenAI's independent, concurrent claim.
quote: Independently and concurrently, an internal model at OpenAI claims to have proven a similar result [Ope26].

claim: Anthropic's bound beats brute-force search on 3-CNF formulas with m=5n clauses only when n exceeds 10^10000 (the exponent is a superscript in the PDF).
quote: Brute force enumeration is already impractical for n = 100, so the improvement of our result does not appear in practical settings.

claim: No person is known to have checked Anthropic's Lean development. It was written and reviewed by AI models.
quote: The Lean development was written by AI models and reviewed by other instances of the same models; at the time of writing no person is known to have checked it; its constant is not explicit.

claim: No machine can check that the Lean statements actually say 'ETH is false'. A human reader has to judge that.
quote: Lean checks the proofs, but no machine checks that this file says what the paper says;

claim: The Lean proofs rely only on Lean's three standard axioms. They are accepted by Lean's kernel, by leanchecker, and by the independent kernel nanoda.
quote: they rest on no axiom beyond Lean’s three standard ones (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). They are accepted by Lean’s kernel, by Lean’s replay checker leanchecker, module by module, and, through Comparator, by the independently implemented kernel nanoda

claim: The Lean proof differs from the printed proof, and AI models, not a mechanical check, compared the two.
quote: AI models, not a mechanical check, compared the Lean proof with the printed one; because of these differences the strictest of them count it as a different proof of the same statement, along the printed route.

claim: Claude's literature search found more than 800 papers whose results depend on ETH or a hypothesis that implies it.
quote: In a literature search carried out by Claude, we found more than 800 papers that prove at least one result of their own only under ETH or under a hypothesis that implies it

claim: The previous record for deterministic 3-SAT was O(1.328^n).
quote: the prior record is O(1.328n ) time for deterministic 3-SAT algorithms [Liu18]

claim: Anthropic's paper says the result does not settle P vs NP and gives no practical algorithm.
quote: However, our result does not bear on the P vs NP question directly, nor does it yield any practical algorithms for NP-complete problems.

claim: OpenAI's preprint, 'The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False', gives a deterministic subexponential counting algorithm for k-CNF and says it refutes ETH.
quote: Our algorithm refutes the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), which postulates that deciding 3-SAT on n variables requires 2Ω(n) time in the worst case.

claim: OpenAI's preprint is dated October 17, 2026, and was revised October 25, 2026.
quote: Date: 17 October 2026, revised 25 October 2026.

claim: OpenAI's math repo holds raw manuscripts from an unnamed internal model, at mixed stages of verification.
quote: This collection includes results at different stages of verification. Not all have accompanying Lean formalizations.

claim: OpenAI released solutions to three major problems, one of them the ETH refutation.
quote: OpenAI released solutions to three blockbuster math problems that have long vexed researchers.

claim: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge suggested OpenAI's solutions built on pre-existing work. Anthropic released its own refutation hours later.
quote: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge suggested that OpenAI was basing its solutions on pre-existing work

claim: Ryan Williams (MIT) says parts of OpenAI's proof look alien.
quote: there are two or three alien-looking parts

claim: Williams does not think OpenAI's algorithm is optimal or the final answer.
quote: I don’t think that OpenAI’s algorithm could possibly be the best algorithm you can get.

claim: Williams says computer scientists should give a bit more weight to P = NP.
quote: Every computer scientist should probably put a little more weight on the plausibility of P = NP, but one's weight may vary,

claim: Per Williams, OpenAI checked whether the result breaks any cryptography and was reasonably confident it does not.
quote: And apparently, they checked, and they were reasonably confident that this didn’t … imply any breaks.

claim: Williams and colleagues released an open letter asking scientists for feedback, and Williams pushed OpenAI to support a conference.
quote: Their first step was to release an open letter calling for feedback from scientists interested in these problems

claim: Williams had earlier called OpenAI's proof release a 'DDOS attack on mathematicians'.
quote: DDOS attack on mathematicians.

claim: Many papers that rely on ETH will need to be revisited.
quote: The durability of ETH has lead to it being included in many scientific papers … that will need to be revisited

claim: Scientific American describes OpenAI's algorithm as only slightly faster than exponential time.
quote: OpenAI’s proof provides an algorithm to solve 3-SAT that is just a tiny bit faster than exponential time, refuting ETH.

claim: OpenAI's three proofs spanned math, physics and computer science (Kakeya, the Yang-Mills existence half, ETH).
quote: dropped three massive proofs that touched on math, physics and computer science

claim: The model behind OpenAI's proofs is proprietary.
quote: The large language model (LLM) that produced the new proofs remains proprietary

claim: Forklog reports that OpenAI's ETH proof was formalized in Lean on October 19. This is not confirmed in OpenAI's preprint.
quote: on October 19 it was formalized in Lean

claim: OpenAI's outside reviewers (Impagliazzo, Paturi, Williams; David Gross for physics) said their participation is not an endorsement.
quote: The researchers emphasized that their participation should not be taken as an endorsement of OpenAI’s conclusion.

claim: Participation in OpenAI's research review groups is voluntary and unpaid.
quote: participation in the research groups will be voluntary and unpaid.

claim: A commenter on John D. Cook's blog notes that a Lean-formalized statement was slightly weaker than the paper's claim, though the subexponential result still holds. Which lab's formalization is meant is unclear.
quote: the formalized statement proved in Lean was slightly weaker than the statement the paper claims to prove
